items.text: Technology doesn’t make you a better thinker. It never has. Habits do.
Easy to say. It feels like AI is making everyone lazier.
Fair worry. Tools change what’s easy, not what’s good. People who check sources still check them with AI in the loop. We’re measuring which habits hold up: pulp.com.ai/research
Our first product is out. Thinkwell is for the people whose work runs on conversation.
quoted: See the world through conversation. Thinkwell keeps every call, hearing and meeting, and writes down what was promised.

why: The reply takes the worry seriously and answers it with one idea and one link. It does not argue a second time.
The quote adds the house’s context to the product’s launch. Pulp amplifies Thinkwell; Thinkwell does not lead with Pulp.
Every post is one idea, under 280 characters.

conversations.title: A product post, a hard question in the comments, and a repost from the house.

items.text: Every hearing, call and coalition meeting ends with a list of who said they’d do what. By Friday, some of it is gone. Thinkwell keeps the conversation, writes down what was promised, and checks claims against the record.
Does it record closed-door meetings?
Only when you ask it to, and everyone in the room can see that it is on. Keeping and sharing are separate choices, and you can delete a session at any time.
Built on research we publish in the open, for the people whose work runs on conversation.

why: The comment is the question every buyer has. The reply answers it plainly, with the consent rules, and no sales line.
The house reposts with one line that adds what only Pulp can add: the research underneath.
The post opens on the reader’s problem, so the first two lines work above the fold.

conversations.title: A person from the team, answering in a community, link only when asked.

items.text: Is there a good way to measure how persuasive an argument is without just asking people whether they agree?

Disclosure: I work at Pulp, and this is our day job. Three things that help: measure change from a stated starting point instead of agreement; score the argument’s structure apart from its delivery; and let the measure abstain when it can’t tell. Happy to share papers if useful.
Why abstain instead of scoring zero?

Zero says “no effect.” Empty says “we couldn’t tell.” Average the zeros in and the cases you couldn’t read disappear, so results look calmer than they are. The methods paper is at pulp.com.ai/research/methods, since you asked.

why: A named person speaks, not a logo, and says who they work for in the first sentence.
The answer is useful on its own. The link comes only after the poster asks a follow-up.
It follows the community’s rules first; the brand second.

conversations.title: A short method thread, then a quote that credits someone else’s work.

items.text: A note on method, since a few people asked. We describe an argument on 48 parameters, 8 channels by 6 dimensions, each from -1 to +1.
When a parameter can’t be read from what was said, it stays empty. Never zero. Zero is a claim; empty is honest.
Rules run first and models second, so the cheap, checkable steps happen before any model call. Methods: pulp.com.ai/research/methods
Careful work on why agreement isn’t the same as persuasion. Worth your time.
quoted: Sample researcher: new paper on measuring opinion change, with open data.

why: Each part stands on its own; the first says why to keep reading; the link waits for the last.
The quote exists to credit someone else, with a reason in one line.
Bluesky’s researchers expect sources, so the thread ends on one.

items.text: What’s a conversation that changed your mind? Not one you won. One that changed you.
My dad and I argued about a zoning vote for a year. He came to the hearing with me and it changed my mind, not his.
That’s the good kind. Changed by showing up, not by being out-argued.
Honestly can’t think of one.
Same for most people. It’s rarer than winning, which is why we study it.

why: Threads rewards replies, so the post is a question people can answer from their own life.

The house never turns a reply into a pitch.
